etymologies.etymologyHTML:
From Middle English custume, borrowed from Anglo-Norman custume, inherited from Latin consuētūdinem, a noun derived from cōnsuēscō, from con- (“with”) + suēscō (“become used or accustomed to”). Doublet of costume and consuetude.

Adjective form circa 1830.

definitions.definition: Frequent repetition of the same behavior; way of behavior common to many; ordinary manner; habitual practice; method of doing, living or behaving.

quote.citation: c. 1599–1602 (date written), William Shakespeare, “The Tragedie of Hamlet, Prince of Denmarke”, in Mr. William Shakespeares Comedies, Histories, & Tragedies […] (First Folio), London:  […]  Isaac Iaggard, and Ed[ward] Blount, published 1623, →OCLC, [Act I, scene iv]:
quote.text: A custom More honour'd in the breach than the observance.

quote.citation: 1611, The Holy Bible, […] (King James Version), London:  […]  Robert Barker, […], →OCLC, Acts 16:20-21:
quote.text: 20  […]  These men being Iewes, do exceedingly trouble our city,21 And teach customes which are not lawfull for vs to receiue, neither to obserue, being Romanes.

quote.citation: a. 1627 (date written), Francis Bacon, “A.D. 1610. Ætat. 50.”, in James Spedding, editor, The Works of Francis Bacon, […]: The Letters and the Life of Francis Bacon […], volume IV, London: Longmans, Green, Reader, and Dyer, published 1858, →OCLC, page 194:
quote.text: For first Mr. Dier's opinion was that the ancient custom for exportation was by the common laws; and goeth furder, that that ancient custom was the custom upon wools, woolfells, and leather.

quote.citation: 1847, Alfred Tennyson, “Part 6”, in The Princess: A Medley, London: Edward Moxon, […], →OCLC:
quote.text: Moved beyond his custom, Gama said

definitions.definition: (collectively) The habitual patrons (i.e. customers) of a business; business support.
(dated outside UK) Habitual buying of goods from one same vendor.

quote.citation: 1710 September 28, Joseph Addison, The Whig Examiner, number 3:
quote.text: Let him have your custom, but not your votes.

definitions.definition: (law) Long-established practice, considered as unwritten law, and resting for authority on long consent. Compare prescription.

quote.citation: 1888, Francis Wharton, A Commentary on the Law of Evidence in Civil Issues, 3rd edition, volume 2, page 188:
quote.text: The distinction between custom and usage it that usage is a fact and custom is a law. There can be usage without custom, but not custom  without usage.

definitions.definition: A custom (made-to-order) piece of art, etc.

quote.text: The rest of the necklace holders finally came in! If you bought a custom from me thank you so much for your patience! I’m gonna try my best to crank them out as fast as possible

quote.citation: 2020 July 28, “Paying for porn: How much is appropriate?”, in Slate Magazine:
quote.text: Oftentimes I have trouble finding enough women to buy customs from. Strangely enough, finding women to take hundreds of dollars for a selfie isn’t as easy as you’d think.

quote.citation: c. 1606–1607 (date written), William Shakespeare, “The Tragedie of Anthonie and Cleopatra”, in Mr. William Shakespeares Comedies, Histories, & Tragedies […] (First Folio), London:  […]  Isaac Iaggard, and Ed[ward] Blount, published 1623, →OCLC, [Act II, scene ii]:
quote.text: Age can not wither her, nor custom staleHer infinite variety.

quote.citation: 1769, Bible, Authorised King James Version, Oxford standard text, Romans, xiii, 7:
quote.text: Render therefore to all their dues: tribute to whom tribute is due; custom to whom custom; fear to whom fear; honour to whom honour.

definitions.definition: Created under particular specifications, specially to fit one's needs: specialized, unique, custom-made.
Own, personal, not standard or premade.
(transitive, obsolete) To make familiar; to accustom.

quote.citation: a. 1771 (written, published posthumously) Thomas Gray, Agrippina
quote.text: Have not forgot your sire; the eye of Rome And the Prætorian camp have long revered, With customed awe the daughter, sister, wife, And mother of their Cæsars

quote.citation: 1605, Francis Bacon, “The Second Booke”, in The Twoo Bookes of Francis Bacon. Of the Proficience and Aduancement of Learning, Diuine and Humane, London:  […]  [Thomas Purfoot and Thomas Creede] for Henrie Tomes, […], →OCLC, folio 52, recto:
quote.text: But yet a man might reply, that if a Shooemaker ſhould haue no Shooes in his Shoppe, but onely worke, as hee is beſpoken, hee ſhould bee weakley cuſtomed.

definitions.definition: (transitive, obsolete) To pay the customs of.

quote.citation: c. 1589–1590 (date written), Christopher Marlo[we], edited by Tho[mas] Heywood, The Famous Tragedy of the Rich Iew of Malta. […], London:  […]  I[ohn] B[eale] for Nicholas Vavasour, […], published 1633, →OCLC, Act I:
quote.text: Barabas, thy ships are safe,Riding in Malta Rhode; and all the merchantsWith other merchandize are safe arriv'd,And have sent me to know whether yourselfWill come and custom them.

quote.citation: 1596, Edmund Spenser, “Book V, Canto II”, in The Faerie Queene. […], part II (books IV–VI), London:  […]  [Richard Field] for William Ponsonby, →OCLC, stanza 7, page 198:
quote.text: For on a Bridge he cuſtometh to fight, / Which is but narrow, but exceeding long; / And in the ſame are many trap fals pight, / Through which the rider downe doth fall through ouerſight.
